title: Environment-Specific Configurations
learning_outcomes: Explain development and production settings in the context of environment-specific configurations.
Apply the lesson concept in a small TypeScript example and describe what the compiler can check.
Identify one limitation or failure case and choose an appropriate runtime check or test when needed.

content.intro: Learn environment-specific configurations through a compact mental model, syllabus-aligned subtopics, a worked example and a practical task. The goal is not to memorize syntax but to know what the type contract guarantees and what evidence is still needed.
content.why_it_matters: Type-level expressiveness is most valuable when it describes real runtime contracts. Keep module mode and tsconfig aligned with the actual Node.js or bundler environment, and treat compiler-version changes as a tested migration.

content_blocks.title: Mental model
content_blocks.text: **Environment-Specific Configurations.** This lesson belongs to **Compiler Configuration and Build Systems**. Start by identifying the problem that environment-specific configurations solves. In TypeScript, separate three questions: what values your program intends to accept, what the compiler can prove from the code, and what must still be checked while the program runs. The last category matters whenever data comes from a user, file, API, storage layer, or an untyped JavaScript dependency.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics and how to use them

items.title: Development and production settings
items.text: For development and production settings, define a measurable success condition, test the ordinary path and a failure path, and record the environment/configuration needed to reproduce the result.

items.title: Shared configuration
items.text: For shared configuration, make the toolchain/configuration explicit and reproducible. Check the configured TypeScript version and use the project command so your result matches the course assumptions.

items.title: Browser, Node.js, and test environments
items.text: For browser, node.js, and test environments, treat incoming values as untrusted until runtime checks establish the required shape. A TypeScript annotation does not validate network, file, database, storage, or user-provided data by itself.

content_blocks.title: Example: Environment-Specific Configurations
content_blocks.expected_output: The configuration enables strict checking and writes generated output to dist. Module settings must match the target runtime and installed compiler version.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This course displays TypeScript examples as static teaching text. The CodeLeaf web playground currently previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; TypeScript is not compiled or executed in the browser preview. For actual compiler feedback, create a local project with a pinned TypeScript version and run `npx tsc --noEmit`. For snippets requiring a browser, Node.js, React/JSX or a test runner, use the matching environment and dependencies.
content_blocks.reset_steps: The lesson example does not modify files or remote systems. If you run it locally, use a disposable project directory, keep package versions recorded, and remove only the generated output you created.
content_blocks.limitations: Static lesson example only. The browser preview is not a TypeScript compiler and does not execute backend, Node.js, React/TSX, test-runner, network or filesystem examples.

content_blocks.title: Compile-time versus runtime
content_blocks.text: Type annotations and most type declarations are erased when TypeScript emits JavaScript. They do not validate external JSON, authorize a user, sanitize HTML, or prevent runtime failures by themselves. Validate trust-boundary inputs and test the behavior.

content.task: Create a small TypeScript example for “Environment-Specific Configurations”. Demonstrate development and production settings, explain your assumption, and include one check that shows the expected behavior. Do not treat a type annotation as runtime validation for external input.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates at least one syllabus subtopic named in this lesson.
The type contract is explicit enough that another learner can explain what it accepts and rejects.
The learner records a failure case and distinguishes compile-time checks from runtime validation.
hints: Start with the syllabus item “Development and production settings” and define the smallest example that demonstrates it.
Ask which part is checked by TypeScript and which part depends on runtime data, the environment or a test.
For external input, start with unknown and validate the required shape before using a domain type.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a successful type check as a runtime guarantee.
common_mistakes.why: Type annotations do not generally validate data after JavaScript starts running.
common_mistakes.fix: Add runtime checks for external input and tests for meaningful failure cases.

common_mistakes.problem: Using any or an assertion to silence a useful diagnostic.
common_mistakes.why: That can hide the exact mismatch the type system would otherwise report.
common_mistakes.fix: Prefer a more precise type or unknown plus narrowing; use assertions only when a verified invariant justifies them.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a compiler setting or runtime example without checking the project environment.
common_mistakes.why: Module resolution, DOM/Node globals, JSX and tool behavior depend on the configured versions and environment.
common_mistakes.fix: Pin the toolchain, match tsconfig to the runtime/bundler, and run the actual project's typecheck and tests.

summary: Environment-Specific Configurations is taught through the subtopics listed in the source syllabus: Development and production settings, Shared configuration, Browser, Node.js, and test environments.
Prefer precise contracts and use compiler diagnostics as evidence, not as a replacement for runtime tests.
Validate untrusted data and describe environment/version assumptions explicitly.
